lines.text: Imports cost 8.1% more than a year ago.
lines.say: Imports cost eight point one percent more than a year ago.

lines.text: That's the September import price report from October 16, the biggest yearly jump since July 2022.
lines.say: That's the September import price report from October sixteenth, the biggest yearly jump since July twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: In January 2026, import prices were down 0.1% from a year earlier.
lines.say: Back in January, import prices were down a tenth of a percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Fuel leads, up 34.5% in a year. But nonfuel imports rose 6% too, the most since April 2022.
lines.say: Fuel leads, up thirty-four point five percent in a year. But nonfuel imports rose six percent too, the most since April twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Imported business equipment, including computers and chips, is up 8.4%, with demand tied to AI investment.
lines.say: Imported business equipment, including computers and chips, is up eight point four percent, with demand tied to AI investment.

lines.text: Import prices are what US buyers pay foreign sellers, before tariffs.
lines.say: Import prices are what US buyers pay foreign sellers, before tariffs.

lines.text: Businesses pay those costs first, and some can get passed along at the pump, on heating bills and in stores.

post.title: Imports cost 8.1% more than a year ago. Here's why
post.ig:
Imports cost 8.1% more than a year ago.
U.S. import prices rose 8.1% from Sept 2025 to Sept 2026, the biggest 12-month jump since July 2022 (BLS, Oct 16, 2026).
Fuel imports: +34.5% in a year. Nonfuel imports: +6.0%, the most since April 2022.
Imported capital goods, including computers and chips, are up 8.4%, with demand tied to AI investment.
Import prices measure what U.S. buyers pay foreign sellers, before tariffs.
Sources: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.
